summary: This document defines the MIB module for configuring and managing OLSRv2. The module is structured into configuration, state, performance information, and notifications.

eli5.summary: This is a list of dials and gauges for adjusting and checking a wireless routing program from a management tool.

questions: how to manage olsrv2 with snmp
what notifications does olsrv2 mib define
subtitle: The SNMP MIB module for configuring, monitoring and getting alerts from routers running OLSRv2 in ad hoc networks.

tldr.problem: Routers running OLSRv2, a link state protocol for mobile ad hoc networks, need a standard way for management tools to configure them and to see their state and performance.
tldr.mechanism: The OLSRv2-MIB module groups objects into configuration, state, performance and notifications, builds on the NHDP-MIB by augmenting its tables, and defines two compliance levels so small routers can implement a subset.
tldr.outcome: Operators can tune OLSRv2 parameters, inspect its information bases and get notifications over SNMP, but the RFC warns that writable objects are sensitive and recommends SNMPv3 security.

today: RFC 7184 is a Proposed Standard and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It manages the OLSRv2 protocol defined in RFC 7181.

sections.title: Introduction and Context
sections.content:
RFC 7184 defines the OLSRv2-MIB, a Management Information Base module for the Optimized Link State Routing Protocol version 2 (OLSRv2, RFC 7181). OLSRv2 is a table-driven, proactive routing protocol: routers exchange topology information periodically. It optimizes classical link state routing with multipoint relays (MPRs), neighbors that each router picks to cover its symmetrically connected 2-hop neighbors, which reduces both flooding and topology information.

MIB objects are generally accessed through the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) and are written in SMIv2. Besides configuration, the module exposes state and performance information useful for troubleshooting. Different compliance levels let implementers use smaller subsets, so the module can run on more constrained routers.
sections.eli5: OLSRv2 is how wireless gadgets work out routes to each other. This document makes a standard list of its dials and gauges.

sections.title: Structure of the MIB Module
sections.content:
The module separates its objects by function. The Configuration Group holds controls for the OLSRv2 instance; the authors tried to support every configuration object in RFC 7181 and follow its constraints and defaults. The State Group reports the current state, designed to cover the full set of Information Bases in RFC 7181. The Performance Group holds counters that can be polled to calculate histories or watch how often sets change. The Notifications Group covers asynchronous event reporting. A conformance section defines minimal and maximal requirements.

OLSRv2 depends on neighborhood information discovered by NHDP (RFC 6130), so an OLSRv2 instance MUST have an associated NHDP instance on the same device. The OLSRv2-MIB aligns with the NHDP-MIB (RFC 6779) and uses the SMIv2 AUGMENTS clause, where possible, to extend its tables. It does not duplicate the System group of the SNMPv2-MIB.
sections.eli5: The dials and gauges sit in labeled drawers: settings, current status, scorecards and alarms. The whole thing hooks onto a neighbor-finding panel it depends on.

sections.title: Tables and Indexing
sections.content:
State is exposed through tables. Five augment NHDP-MIB tables and are indexed by NHDP indexes such as nhdpIfIndex: olsrv2InterfaceTable, olsrv2IibLinkSetTable, olsrv2Iib2HopSetTable, olsrv2NibNeighborSetTable and olsrv2InterfacePerfTable.

The others have their own indexes built from address type and address pairs: olsrv2LibOrigSetTable (recently used originator addresses), olsrv2LibLocAttNetSetTable (local attached networks), olsrv2TibAdRemoteRouterSetTable (remote routers sending TC messages), olsrv2TibRouterTopologySetTable (links between routers), olsrv2TibRoutableAddressTopologySetTable, olsrv2TibAttNetworksSetTable and olsrv2TibRoutingSetTable, which holds the first hop along a selected path to each known destination.

Link metrics use a compressed form following RFC 7181: values range from 1 to 16776960, with 0 reserved for the unknown metric. The metric type is defined through the IANAolsrv2LinkMetricType-MIB.
sections.eli5: Each table is like a notebook: one lists neighbors, one lists routers far away, one lists which way to go for each place.

sections.title: Configuration Objects and Their Risks
sections.content:
Configuration objects include olsrv2AdminStatus, olsrv2InterfaceAdminStatus, the originator address, TC message timing (olsrv2TcInterval, olsrv2TcMinInterval), hold times for the information bases, jitter values, olsrv2TcHopLimit, willingness to be an MPR (olsrv2WillRouting, olsrv2WillFlooding) and olsrv2LinkMetricType.

The Security Considerations explain how bad settings hurt. A TC interval that is too high a rate could amount to a denial of service by overloading interface resources; too low and OLSRv2 may not converge fast enough. A TC hop limit that is too low stops messages from reaching distant routers. Hold times that are too low make information expire quickly. Willingness of WILL_NEVER (0) means the router forwards no TC messages and refuses MPR selection, while WILL_ALWAYS (15) makes it preferred and may attract more traffic. Changing the link metric type invalidates all recorded link metric information, and routers that do not know the new type cannot route to or through that router.
sections.eli5: The dials are powerful. Turn one too far and the router either shouts too much, forgets too quickly, or stops helping its neighbors.

sections.title: Performance Counters and Notifications
sections.content:
Frequent recalculation of the Routing Set or the MPRs can hurt OLSRv2 performance. The Performance Group offers counters such as TC messages transmitted and received, triggered, periodic and forwarded TC transmissions, and the counts of Routing Set and MPR set recalculations, which an administrator can poll to spot unusual topology changes.

Four notifications are defined: olsrv2RouterStatusChange, olsrv2OrigIpAddrChange, olsrv2RoutingSetRecalculationCountChange and olsrv2MPRSetRecalculationCountChange. The two recalculation notifications fire when a significant number of recalculations occur in a short time. They SHOULD be generated no more than once per window, and the administrator chooses the threshold and window values through four read-write objects.
sections.eli5: Counters tell you how often the router had to redo its homework, and an alarm rings only if it happens too often too fast.

sections.title: Compliance Levels
sections.content: Two compliance statements let constrained routers take part. olsrv2BasicCompliance mandates only the configuration objects group. olsrv2FullCompliance mandates the configuration, state, performance, notification objects and notifications groups.
sections.eli5: Small gadgets can offer just the settings drawer. Bigger ones offer everything, including gauges and alarms.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Read-write and read-create objects are sensitive, since unprotected SET operations can disrupt the network. Some readable objects are sensitive too: olsrv2TibRouterTopologySetTable lists router addresses in the MANET and could help an adversary attack other members without doing their own discovery.

Because the augmenting tables mirror NHDP-MIB tables, access control for each pair SHOULD be consistent (the RFC says this is RECOMMENDED). The RFC notes that MANETs are often used for emergency services or military tactical applications, and RECOMMENDS full use of SNMPv3 authentication and privacy. Implementations SHOULD provide SNMPv3 security features, and those claiming SNMPv3 compliance MUST support the User-based Security Model with the AES cipher. Deploying SNMP versions before SNMPv3 is NOT RECOMMENDED.
sections.eli5: Anyone who can flip the dials can break the network, and the maps show attackers who is out there. So only trusted people should be allowed in, with a secret handshake.

sections.title: Where This Module Applies
sections.content:
The applicability statement says SNMP, and therefore this module, suits only a subset of MANET deployments: routers with enough memory and CPU to run SNMP, a defined network management system, an NMS reachable most of the time (so the topology should be only moderately dynamic), and a wireless channel with enough bandwidth and tolerable loss rates.

Examples that fit are community networks with non-mobile routers, topology changes from varying link quality, and a predefined gateway that could also act as NMS. More constrained MANETs may need different management protocols. IANA maintains the IANAolsrv2LinkMetricType-MIB, and the module uses the assigned identifier { mib-2 219 }.
sections.eli5: This control panel only works when the gadgets are strong enough and can mostly reach the person holding the remote.
